evidence_location: +13 mV relative to the forehead, and blink potentials caused by the eyelids sliding over the positively charged cornea: Lins 1993 abstract (sentences 3-4); the same mechanism is in the Picton 2000 abstract, Conclusions. Lid acting as a sliding electrode that short-circuits the cornea to the scalp, and blink topography mostly over frontal electrodes: Plöchl 2012, Results, section 'Eyelid-induced artifacts', first paragraph. Not a muscle signal: Plöchl 2012, Discussion, 'Eye- and eyelid movement artifacts', closing paragraph just before 'Correction of eye movement artifacts' (ocular muscle contribution, including phasic activity during blinking, called negligible, citing Mowrer et al. 1935); also Kovach 2011, Discussion, subsection 'Comparison to previous reports'. Intracranial blink artifacts resembling electro-oculogram (EOG) components from the corneoretinal potential and blink-related conductivity change rather than muscle depolarization: Kovach 2011, Discussion, 'Comparison to previous reports' (summarising Ball et al. 2009). Small burst above 30 Hz at blink initiation in fronto-temporal magnetoencephalography (MEG) sensors, and the muscle-plus-eyelid attribution: Bardouille 2006 abstract, Results and Conclusions (the quote is from the Conclusions).
quote: The anterior activation is likely a combination of muscle contraction and eyelid currents.
discrepancy: (1) No cited source says the lid muscle adds AT MOST a small burst. Bardouille et al. attribute the anterior (periorbital) activation as a whole, which in their Results comprises increased 1-18 Hz and 32-64 Hz activity in and around the orbits over the 400 ms after blink onset, to a combination of muscle contraction and eyelid currents; they do not cap the muscle share at a brief burst. The nearest support for a small muscle role is Plöchl et al. calling the ocular muscle contribution negligible, which concerns electroencephalography (EEG) artifacts and rests on Mowrer et al. 1935, not on the magnetoencephalography (MEG) burst. (2) The claim narrows the attribution: in the abstract the burst above 30 Hz is a sensor-level observation reported alongside a large slow wave of about 400 ms, and the muscle-plus-eyelid explanation is given for the anterior activation generally, not specifically for the burst (full text inaccessible, so a burst-specific attribution in the Discussion could not be checked). (3) The abstract says only muscle contraction; it does not name the lid-closing muscle (orbicularis oculi), and the blinks studied were voluntary (8 adults). (4) Minor: the intracranial sentence is Kovach et al. summarising Ball et al. 2009 (prefrontal electrocorticography (ECoG)), with the mechanism resting on older citations (Arden 1962, Kris 1958, Miles 1939); the claim's 'have been described' wording is accurate, but Kovach is a secondary source, and Kovach's own Introduction lists Ball's blink contamination among muscle artifacts, in tension with its Discussion. All other parts (+13 mV, eyelid mechanism, sliding electrode, mostly frontal, not a muscle signal) match the sources.
suggested_fix: Replace the last sentence with: 'Muscle activity is thought to add little to the scalp blink artifact. In magnetoencephalography (MEG), voluntary blinks produce a large slow wave lasting about 400 ms and a small burst above 30 Hz at blink onset; the authors attribute the activity around the eyes to a combination of muscle contraction and eyelid currents.' Optionally cite the primary intracranial study directly: Ball T, Kern M, Mutschler I, Aertsen A, Schulze-Bonhage A (2009). Signal quality of simultaneously recorded invasive and non-invasive EEG. NeuroImage 46(3):708-716. doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.02.028
